title: Cellular Composition, Not Transcriptional Reprogramming, Drives the COVID-19 Brain Aging Signature in Postmortem Frontal Cortex
content: Severe COVID-19 produces a frontal cortex transcriptome that resembles brain aging. What remains unresolved is the regulatory architecture behind that signature, and whether the bulk RNA-seq signal reflects cell-intrinsic transcriptional reprogramming or shifts in cellular composition. We addressed both questions in a single integrated analysis of GSE188847 (n = 54 postmortem frontal cortex samples; 22 COVID-19, 23 age- and sex-matched controls, 9 ICU/ventilated non-COVID controls). DESeq2 differential expression with apeglm shrinkage identified 7,079 differentially expressed genes between COVID-19 and control samples (4,086 up, 2,993 down). Gene set enrichment analysis recovered 1,708 GO Biological Process terms, with humoral and innate immune programs activated and synaptic transmission, axonal development and oxidative phosphorylation suppressed. VIPER master regulator analysis using DoRothEA confidence A/B/C regulons identified 31 transcription factors with significantly altered activity. NF-κB (RELA, NFKB1) and IFN/JAK-STAT (STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, IRF2) emerged as dominant activated regulators. REST, the canonical neuronal-aging longevity factor, reached significance (NES = +3.29, padj = 0.016) and showed coordinated suppression of 8 of 11 neuronal-identity targets including BDNF, VGF and TUBB3. BRETIGEA cell-type deconvolution revealed neuronal depletion alongside astrocyte, microglia, oligodendrocyte progenitor and endothelial expansion, a five-cell-type neurovascular response. Composition-corrected DESeq2 collapsed 98.3% of the original differential expression signal: of 6,603 symbol-mapped DEGs, only 110 (1.7%) survived adjustment for neuronal and astrocyte composition. The COVID-19 frontal cortex transcriptome is therefore dominantly compositional rather than cell-intrinsic, with implications for therapeutic prioritization in post-acute neurological sequelae.
